result.summary: Aegisthus is killed offstage, and Orestes confronts Clytaemestra, who pleads for her life; urged by Pylades to obey Loxias, he kills her. He displays the bloody robe that trapped Agamemnon, justifies himself, then is driven out by visions of the avenging Furies as the Chorus laments the house's cycle of suffering.

scenes.title: Chorus prays; Aegisthus cries out
scenes.summary: The Chorus prays for Orestes' success and hears Aegisthus' death cry from within, then withdraws.
scenes.stakes: The fate of the house of Agamemnon hangs on whether Orestes defeats his enemies.

scenes.title: The servant raises the alarm
scenes.summary: A servant announces Aegisthus' death; Clytaemestra calls for an axe and the dead Aegisthus is revealed with Orestes.
scenes.stakes: Clytaemestra faces defeat and death at the hands of her avenging son.

scenes.title: Orestes confronts his mother
scenes.summary: Clytaemestra pleads; Pylades reminds Orestes of Loxias' oracle, and Orestes drives her inside to die.
scenes.stakes: Clytaemestra's life; Orestes risks the horror of matricide against the wrath of the gods if he refuses.

scenes.title: Chorus exults in justice
scenes.summary: The Chorus rejoices that the house is freed, crediting Loxias and Justice.

scenes.title: Orestes displays the robe
scenes.summary: Orestes shows the net-like robe that bound Agamemnon, justifies the killing, and announces his exile to Loxias' shrine.
scenes.stakes: Orestes fears pollution, exile and his own failing wits.

scenes.title: Orestes flees the Furies
scenes.summary: Orestes sees the avenging Furies and rushes out; the Chorus laments the third storm to strike the house.
scenes.stakes: Orestes is hunted by his mother's Furies and madness.

alias_notes.explanation: Loxias is a title of Apollo as oracular god; Orestes addresses him as Apollo at sentence 182.

notable_quotes.reason: The servant's riddling cry that the dead Agamemnon is killing the living.
Orestes' hesitation before matricide, answered by Pylades.
Orestes alone sees the Furies as madness begins.

analysis.text: Vengeance fulfils divine command yet brings pollution, showing justice as a cycle of bloodshed that leaves even the avenger tormented.
The play dramatizes the move from blood-feud toward law; the Furies' appearance sets up the court of the Eumenides.

legacy.text: Orestes' pursuit by the Furies after killing his mother became a lasting image of guilt, reworked by Sartre in The Flies (1943) and by Eugene O'Neill in Mourning Becomes Electra (1931).

fun_facts.text: The Libation-Bearers is the middle play of the Oresteia, which won first prize at the Athenian Dionysia in 458 BC.

language_notes.text: Zeus is invoked as the supreme god and guardian of justice, whose will underlies Orestes' act of vengeance.
The Chorus weighs two outcomes: Orestes' failure destroys the house, or his victory brings freedom and his inheritance. 'Blades that lay men low' is a poetic phrase for swords.
'Cope with two' means face two opponents at once: Aegisthus and Clytemnestra. 'Bout' casts the struggle as a contest.
The Chorus wants to keep clear of the killing while its outcome is uncertain, so that they cannot be blamed for it.
The servant says the door needs a strong arm, but not to help Aegisthus, who is past saving. He means help is useless for the dead.
"Nigh the razor's edge" means her neck is close to the blade; the servant predicts her death at the stroke, which she deserves.
"The dead are killing the living" refers to Agamemnon, whom Clytaemestra and Aegisthus killed. His son Orestes now avenges him.
"By guile we are to perish even as we slew" recalls how Agamemnon was trapped in a robe and murdered by trickery.
A battle-axe is a double-edged weapon. She wants to fight, and the axe recalls the weapon associated with her husband's murder.
"He yonder" refers to Aegisthus, whom Orestes has just killed offstage; he is saying Aegisthus is dealt with.
Loxias is a title of Apollo, whose oracle at Pytho (Delphi) commanded Orestes to avenge his father; the "covenant" is Orestes' sworn promise to obey.
Clytaemestra blames Fate, as she and the Chorus do elsewhere in the trilogy, to deflect her own responsibility for Agamemnon's murder.
A parent's curse was believed to summon the Furies, avengers of wrongs against kin; this foreshadows Orestes' later torment.
Orestes says he was 'sold': sent away to Strophius, he claims, in effect for a price, not as a loved son. 'Freeborn sire' stresses Agamemnon's status.
Orestes will not openly say she took the price of his sale; 'outright' means plainly, and the refusal still hints at the charge.
'Sleuth-hounds' are the Furies (Erinyes), pictured as hunting dogs that track down those who shed kindred blood.
She feels she is wailing before a tomb: pleading with Orestes is as useless as mourning a dead man, an echo of Agamemnon's grave.
Refers to her dream, in which she bore a serpent that drew blood with her milk, which Orestes now identifies with himself.
'Prophet' means the dream truly foretold what would happen; the text is slightly garbled here.
"These" are Clytemnestra and Aegisthus, whose deaths the Chorus pities even while approving; "twofold downfall" means both fell together.
"The eye of the house" means Orestes, the surviving heir, whose life keeps the family line from being extinguished.
Priam and his sons fell when Troy was sacked, punishment for Paris's wrong against Menelaus. The Chorus compares that retribution to this one.
Pytho is the older name of Delphi; its god is Apollo, who commanded Orestes to avenge his father.
The "daughter of Zeus" is Justice (Dike), here personified as guiding Orestes' hand.
Loxias is a title of Apollo as oracle, whose shrine stood on Parnassus at Delphi.
"Guileless guile" is a paradox: Orestes' deceit was sanctioned by the god, so it is deceit without wrong.
Fortune is likened to dice, a game of chance: the throw will now fall favourably for the household.
"Supplant" is evidently a misprint for "suppliant", one seeking protection; the olive branch and wool-wreathed bough marked this status.
Bitterly ironic: Orestes calls Clytemnestra and Aegisthus 'loving' because they lie dead together, faithful to their pledge in death.
'The Father... the Sun' is the sun-god, who sees everything and so can witness the crime; Orestes distinguishes him from his own father.
'Zone' means girdle or belt; 'beneath her zone' means in her womb.
'Bier' is the frame on which a corpse is carried or laid.
'Vesture' means garment; 'tinctures' are dyes, and 'broidered' means embroidered.
'Wight' means person; 'scatheless' means unharmed.
Loxias is Apollo as god of prophecy; Pytho is Delphi, where his oracle commanded Orestes to avenge his father.
'Earth's central seat' is Delphi, regarded as the navel of the world; the 'imperishable' fire is the sacred hearth there.
"Yoke not thy tongue to ill-omened speech" means do not speak words of bad omen; the Greeks believed such words could bring misfortune.
The two serpents are Clytemnestra and Aegisthus, whom Orestes killed; the Chorus calls them snakes to justify the deed.
Gorgons were monstrous winged women with snakes for hair, whose gaze turned men to stone. Orestes uses them to describe the Furies.
"Stoled" means robed; a stole is a long flowing garment.
"Sleuth-hounds" are tracking dogs; the Furies hunt down those who shed kindred blood.
Loxias is a title of Apollo, whose oracle commanded the killing and who purified murderers at Delphi.
"Children slain for food" refers to Atreus feeding Thyestes his own children's flesh; the king murdered in a bath is Agamemnon.
"Somewhence" means from some unknown source; the Chorus is unsure whether Orestes is a savior or a new doom.

context_notes.text: Orestes has returned from exile to avenge his father Agamemnon, killed by Clytemnestra and Aegisthus. His inheritance is the throne of Argos.
Aegisthus, Clytemnestra's lover, helped murder Agamemnon and now rules Argos. His cry from within shows Orestes has struck him.
The women's door led to the women's quarters of a Greek house, where Clytaemestra would be found, apart from the men's rooms.
Pylades is Orestes' loyal friend and companion. He has been mostly silent, but speaks later in this play.
Aegisthus was Clytaemestra's lover and co-murderer of Agamemnon, and had ruled Argos with her during Orestes' exile.
Pylades is Orestes' friend and has been silent so far; his only lines in the play are this one, and they decide the matter.
Clytaemestra claims she sent young Orestes to a friendly host, Strophius of Phocis, for his safety, not to cast him out.
Orestes fears the Furies of his murdered father, whose claim to vengeance he must satisfy, as Apollo (Loxias) commanded.
Purification rites were needed to cleanse a house of bloodshed. Here they anticipate Orestes' own cleansing, though the Furies will soon challenge it.
The robe is the one in which Clytemnestra and Aegisthus trapped Agamemnon in his bath, displayed here as evidence of their crime.
Orestes has just killed his mother Clytemnestra and her lover Aegisthus, who together murdered Agamemnon.
Agamemnon was trapped in a robe or net while bathing on returning from Troy, then struck down.
A suppliant carried an olive branch wound with wool as a sign of seeking sanctuary and purification.
The Furies (Erinyes) were goddesses who pursued those who killed their own kin, especially a mother.
The Chorus counts three storms on the house of Atreus: Thyestes' feast, Agamemnon's murder, and now Orestes' act of vengeance and its consequences.

literary_notes.text: The Chorus addresses Zeus directly, repeating his name to show anxiety and a sudden loss for words at the crisis.
Kindling a 'flaming light' stands for hope and deliverance from tyranny, set against the image of blood-stained blades.
Aegisthus' offstage cry tells the audience of his death before the Chorus can interpret it, heightening suspense.
The servant's repeated cries of woe, counted aloud, convey rising panic and heighten urgency.
The riddle of the dead killing the living is a paradox. It makes the avenging of Agamemnon feel like his own dead hand striking.
Clytaemestra instantly decodes the riddle and calls for a weapon, showing her quick wits and defiant courage even as her world collapses.
Her trickery is turned against her. The guile she used on Agamemnon now returns, giving the plot a fitting poetic justice.
Clytaemestra's appeal to the nursing breast and toothless infant is an emotional plea meant to recall the mother-child bond.
Pylades' brief, forceful command shows divine obligation outweighing pity, and tips Orestes from hesitation to resolve.
Orestes turns her own excuse of Fate against her, answering her evasion with the same logic.
Clytaemestra appeals to pity and to her own widowhood, though she herself caused it; this shows her self-justifying manipulation.
Orestes turns her warning back on her: by killing Agamemnon she has brought her own death upon herself.
Calling Orestes a serpent she nursed makes him a monstrous child, fulfilling the earlier dream imagery.
The balanced phrasing 'slewest whom thou shouldst not; suffer what should not be' states retributive justice, an eye for an eye.
Orestes and Pylades, or the two avengers, are imagined as a "twofold lion", conveying fierce, predatory force.
Justice is given a name, parentage and a guiding hand, making the abstract principle an active divine agent.
The repeated call to triumph (also at 115) gives the ode a ritual, song-like structure and emphasizes celebration.
Light stands for deliverance, and the "curb" is a bridle image: the house was held in tyrannical restraint like a horse.
The Chorus addresses the palace itself as if it could rise, joining the house's fate to its restored fortunes.
Orestes imagines Clytemnestra so venomous that her mere touch would rot flesh, exaggerating her vileness.
A run of questions shows Orestes searching for a word vile enough for the robe, building his accusation.
The robe is called a hunting-net, casting Agamemnon as trapped prey and the murder as a base ambush.
Orestes compares his unruly mind to a charioteer losing control of his team, foreshadowing his coming madness.
Killing the two is "lopping off the heads" of serpents, casting the murders as a heroic labor that frees Argos.
Orestes likens the Furies to Gorgons, conveying their horror through his own vivid, fearful vision.
Only Orestes sees the Furies, showing his guilt is real to him though invisible to the Chorus; the audience senses what is coming.
Family misfortune is a tempest that bursts and runs its course, picturing the curse as a recurring natural force.
The Chorus closes with an unanswered question, leaving the cycle of violence unresolved and foreshadowing further suffering.
